name: Chandrasekhar-Xanthopoulos Colliding Plane Waves
description: Two plane gravitational waves colliding head on in flat space, each an impulse with a shock wave behind it, their polarizations out of line. Where both have passed the spacetime is locally Kerr's between its horizons, and the waves focus each other onto a Killing-Cauchy horizon with the curvature finite.
convention: No coordinate carries dimensions of time, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
history: What happens when two gravitational waves meet head on? The simplest case fell in 1971 to K. A. Khan and Roger Penrose: two impulsive plane waves in flat space, each focusing the other until the curvature blows up along a spacelike singularity [khan1971]. Six years later Yavuz Nutku and Mustafa Halil turned the polarization of one wave against the other, and the singularity stayed [nutku1977, chandrasekhar1984ferrari]. At first, Jerry Griffiths wrote, "it was widely believed that the collision of plane waves would necessarily produce a future space-like curvature singularity" [griffiths1991].¶Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar came to the problem from black holes, and the two problems turned out to be close cousins. A spacetime of colliding plane waves has two spacelike Killing vectors, a rotating black hole has one timelike and one spacelike, and with Valeria Ferrari he showed in 1984 that the vacuum equations of the first reduce to a single equation of the Ernst type, as those of the second do [chandrasekhar1984ferrari, griffiths1991]. Its simplest solution, $E = p\eta + iq\mu$ with $p^2 + q^2 = 1$, led them directly to the collision of Nutku and Halil [chandrasekhar1984ferrari]. That same function is the Ernst potential of Roy Kerr's rotating black hole [griffiths1991, kerr1963]. For colliding waves the Ernst function can be read in two ways, as holding the metric functions themselves or as a potential for them [griffiths1991].¶The second reading was taken up in 1986 by Chandrasekhar and Basilis Xanthopoulos, and it turns the same function into a new collision [chandrasekhar1986, griffiths1991]. Where both waves have passed, their spacetime is "locally isometric to the Kerr space-time in a region interior to the ergosphere" [chandrasekhar1986]. Picture the inside of a rotating black hole between its two horizons, where the radius $r$ is a time: the waves collide on $r = M$ and $\theta = \pi/2$, with the hole's mass $M$ written as a length, and Kerr's $t$ and $\phi$ are the two directions along the wave fronts, $\phi$ unrolled to run over the whole line [griffiths1991, gurtug2015]. The spin of the hole is the misalignment of the waves, $a = qM$, and each incoming wave is an impulse with a shock wave behind it [griffiths1991, chandrasekhar1986].¶Khan and Penrose's waves focus each other onto a singularity, and on the same surface these waves meet "a null surface which acts like an event horizon" [chandrasekhar1986]. It is the inner horizon of Kerr, where the curvature stays finite, and the spacetime continues through it [griffiths1991]. On the far side Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos found timelike curvature singularities "along two hyperbolic arcs", "reminiscent of the ring singularity of the Kerr metric" [chandrasekhar1986]. The singularity is timelike, so in Griffiths's words "it would be missed by most observers" [griffiths1991]. A second pair of waves, found by Cornelius Hoenselaers and Frederick Ernst in 1990, collides on the same plane and runs outward to Kerr's outer horizon, with the asymptotically flat exterior of the black hole beyond it [hoenselaers1990, griffiths1991]. With the polarizations aligned, $q = 0$, the spin goes, the region is a piece of the inside of Schwarzschild's black hole, and the horizon of Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos becomes a curvature singularity [griffiths1991, ferrari1988].¶Would a real collision end on a horizon? The first answer was Ulvi Yurtsever's, in 1987: Killing-Cauchy horizons in plane symmetric spacetimes are unstable against plane symmetric perturbations, and generic colliding plane waves "are likely to have spacelike singularities without Killing-Cauchy horizons" [yurtsever1987]. Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos tested their own horizon that November by coupling the waves to matter: an electromagnetic field leaves the horizon in place, and null dust "prevents the development of horizons and allows only the development of space-like singularities" [chandrasekhar1987]. For incoming waves with constant aligned polarizations Griffiths confirmed in 2005 that bounded perturbations of the waves themselves destroy such a horizon [griffiths2005killing]. Beyond the horizon the continuation is one of many, each fixed by extra data that the incoming waves do not carry [griffiths1991].¶Real waves are never plane, and a plane wave is infinite in extent, which limits what these collisions say about real ones [griffiths1991]. Frans Pretorius and William East gave the waves a finite extent in 2018, sourcing each with a distribution of null particles, and ran the head on collision numerically [pretorius2018]. A black hole formed promptly and held most of the energy, with $15 \pm 1\%$ of it radiated away as gravitational waves [pretorius2018].

related.text: Where both waves have passed, the metric is Kerr's between its two horizons in the coordinates of Boyer and Lindquist, with $r = m(1 - p\eta)$, $\cos\theta = \mu$, and $a = mq$, and with $t$ and $\phi$ running along the wave fronts [chandrasekhar1986, griffiths1991, boyer1967].

The same collision with waves that are impulses alone and polarizations aligned. Khan and Penrose's waves focus each other onto a curvature singularity on the surface where these waves meet a horizon, $\eta = 1$ here and $u^2 + v^2 = 1$ in their null coordinates [khan1971, chandrasekhar1986].
Two electromagnetic shock waves that also end on a Killing-Cauchy horizon. Between their fronts lies the Bertotti-Robinson universe, where these waves have Kerr [bell1974, griffiths1991].
With the polarizations aligned, $q = 0$, the metric between the fronts is Schwarzschild's inside its horizon, from $r = m$ down to the singularity at $r = 0$ [griffiths1991, ferrari1988].
Each incoming wave alone is a plane wave of this family, an impulse with a shock wave behind it [chandrasekhar1986, griffiths1991].
Ahead of both waves, where $u < 0$ and $v < 0$, the spacetime is flat [griffiths1991].

The inner horizon of a black hole under perturbation. Ulvi Yurtsever took the Cauchy horizons of plane symmetric spacetimes, the kind these waves end on, as a simpler model of the same problem [yurtsever1993].

coordinates.name: Chandrasekhar-Xanthopoulos

parameters.description: A length that sets the scale of the collision; between the fronts it is the mass of Kerr's metric, $GM/c^2$
An angle with $0 < \alpha < \pi/2$ that sets how far the polarizations of the two waves are out of line; they are aligned at $\alpha = 0$
Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos's $p$, with $p^2 + q^2 = 1$
Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos's $q$, the spin of Kerr's metric in units of its mass, $a/m$
Kerr's radius in units of $m$, which falls from one on the collision to $1 - p$ on the horizon
Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos's $X$, Kerr's $r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta$ in units of $m^2$
Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos's $Y$, equal to $p^2(1 - \eta^2) + q^2(1 - \mu^2)$, which is $X$ times the squared length of the Killing vector $\partial_x$

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(\eta, \mu, x, y)$ of Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos where both waves have passed, with $\eta$ and $\mu$ dimensionless and $x$ and $y$ lengths across the wave fronts, and write $\rho$, $X$, and $Y$ as the parameters define them. The parameters $p = \cos\alpha$ and $q = \sin\alpha$ obey $p^2 + q^2 = 1$, and $m$ is a length. With null coordinates $u$ and $v$ that vanish on the two wave fronts, $\eta = \sin(u + v)$ and $\mu = \sin(u - v)$, and ahead of one wave or both, where $u < 0$ or $v < 0$, the metric is this one with $u$ or $v$ set to zero.
geodesics: \ddot{\eta} - \dfrac{q^2\,\rho\,\mu^2 - q^2\,\rho - q^2\,\mu^2 + \rho^2}{p\,X\left(1 - \eta^2\right)}\dot{\eta}^2 + \dfrac{2q^2\,\mu}{X}\dot{\eta}\dot{\mu} - \dfrac{p\,\rho\left(1 - \eta^2\right)}{X\left(1 - \mu^2\right)}\dot{\mu}^2 - \dfrac{p\left(q\,\mu + \rho\right)\left(q\,\mu - \rho\right)\left(1 - \eta^2\right)}{X^3\,m^2}\dot{x}^2 + \dfrac{2q\left(\mu^2 + 1\right)\left(q\,\mu + \rho\right)\left(q\,\mu - \rho\right)\left(1 - \eta^2\right)}{X^3\,m^2}\dot{x}\dot{y} - \dfrac{\left(q^4\,\rho\,\mu^4 - q^4\,\rho\,\mu^6 + q^4\,\mu^2 + 2q^4\,\mu^4 + q^4\,\mu^6 + 2q^2\,\rho^3\,\mu^2 - 2q^2\,\rho^3\,\mu^4 - 2q^2\,\rho^2\,\mu^2 - q^2\,\rho^2\,\mu^4 - q^2\,\rho^2 - \rho^5\,\mu^2 + \rho^5\right)\left(1 - \eta^2\right)}{p\,X^3\,m^2}\dot{y}^2 = 0

\ddot{x} + \dfrac{2\left(q + \rho\right)\left(q - \rho\right)\left(q\,\mu + \rho\right)\left(q\,\mu - \rho\right)}{p\,X^2\left(1 - \eta^2\right)}\dot{\eta}\dot{x} + \dfrac{2q\left(2q^4\,\rho\,\mu^4 - q^4\,\mu^2 - q^4\,\mu^4 + 4q^2\,\rho^3\,\mu^2 - q^2\,\rho^2\,\mu^4 + q^2\,\rho^2 + 2\rho^5 - 3\rho^4\,\mu^2 - 3\rho^4\right)}{p^2\,X^2\left(1 - \eta^2\right)}\dot{\eta}\dot{y} - \dfrac{4q^2\,\rho\,\mu\left(\mu^2 + 1\right)}{X^2\left(1 - \mu^2\right)}\dot{\mu}\dot{x} - \dfrac{4q\,\mu\left(q^4\,\mu^4 + 2q^2\,\rho^2\,\mu^2 - 2q^2\,\rho\,\mu^2 - q^2\,\rho\,\mu^4 - q^2\,\rho + \rho^4\right)}{p\,X^2\left(1 - \mu^2\right)}\dot{\mu}\dot{y} = 0

coordinates.name: Time and Space

parameters.description: A length that sets the scale of the collision; between the fronts it is the mass of Kerr's metric, $GM/c^2$
An angle with $0 < \alpha < \pi/2$ that sets how far the polarizations of the two waves are out of line; they are aligned at $\alpha = 0$
Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos's $p$, with $p^2 + q^2 = 1$
Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos's $q$, the spin of Kerr's metric in units of its mass, $a/m$
Kerr's radius in units of $m$, which falls from one on the collision to $1 - p$ on the horizon
Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos's $X$, Kerr's $r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta$ in units of $m^2$
Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos's $Y$, equal to $p^2\cos^2\psi + q^2\cos^2\lambda$, which is $X$ times the squared length of the Killing vector $\partial_x$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\psi, \lambda, x, y)$ where both waves have passed, with $\psi$ and $\lambda$ dimensionless and $x$ and $y$ lengths across the wave fronts, and write $\rho$, $X$, and $Y$ as the parameters define them. The parameters $p = \cos\alpha$ and $q = \sin\alpha$ obey $p^2 + q^2 = 1$, and $m$ is a length. With null coordinates $u$ and $v$ that vanish on the two wave fronts, $\psi = u + v$ and $\lambda = u - v$, and ahead of one wave or both, where $u < 0$ or $v < 0$, the metric is this one with $u$ or $v$ set to zero.
geodesics: \ddot{x} + \dfrac{2\left(q + \rho\right)\left(q - \rho\right)\left(q\sin\lambda + \rho\right)\left(q\sin\lambda - \rho\right)}{p\,X^2\cos\psi}\dot{\psi}\dot{x} + \dfrac{2q\left(2q^4\,\rho\sin^4\lambda - q^4\sin^2\lambda - q^4\sin^4\lambda + 4q^2\,\rho^3\sin^2\lambda - q^2\,\rho^2\sin^4\lambda + q^2\,\rho^2 + 2\rho^5 - 3\rho^4\sin^2\lambda - 3\rho^4\right)}{p^2\,X^2\cos\psi}\dot{\psi}\dot{y} - \dfrac{4q^2\,\rho\left(\sin^2\lambda + 1\right)\sin\lambda}{X^2\cos\lambda}\dot{\lambda}\dot{x} - \dfrac{4q\left(q^4\sin^4\lambda + 2q^2\,\rho^2\sin^2\lambda - 2q^2\,\rho\sin^2\lambda - q^2\,\rho\sin^4\lambda - q^2\,\rho + \rho^4\right)\sin\lambda}{p\,X^2\cos\lambda}\dot{\lambda}\dot{y} = 0

coordinates.name: Boyer-Lindquist

parameters.description: A length that sets the scale of the collision; between the fronts it is the mass of Kerr's metric, $GM/c^2$
Spin parameter of Kerr's metric, a length with $0 < a < m$, equal to $mq$
Kerr's $\Sigma$, equal to $m^2X$
Kerr's horizon function, negative between the horizons $r_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 - a^2}$ and zero on them

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Boyer and Lindquist for Kerr's metric between its horizons, with $t$ a length, and write $\Sigma$ and $\Delta$ as the parameters define them. With $a = mq$ they are $r = m(1 - p\eta)$, $\cos\theta = \mu$, $t = x - 2qy/p$, and $\phi = -y/(mp)$, so $\phi$ runs over the whole line.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{m\,\Delta\left(a\cos\theta + r\right)\left(a\cos\theta - r\right)}{\Sigma^3}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{2m\,a\,\Delta\left(a\cos\theta + r\right)\left(a\cos\theta - r\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^3}\dot{t}\dot{\phi} + \dfrac{m\,a^2\cos^2\theta - m\,r^2 - a^2\,r\cos^2\theta + a^2\,r}{\Sigma\,\Delta}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{2a^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\Sigma}\dot{r}\dot{\theta} - \dfrac{r\,\Delta}{\Sigma}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\Delta\left(m\,a^4\cos^2\theta - m\,a^4\cos^4\theta + m\,a^2\,r^2\cos^2\theta - m\,a^2\,r^2 + a^4\,r\cos^4\theta + 2a^2\,r^3\cos^2\theta + r^5\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^3}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Ingoing Kerr

parameters.description: A length that sets the scale of the collision; between the fronts it is the mass of Kerr's metric, $GM/c^2$
Spin parameter of Kerr's metric, a length with $0 < a < m$, equal to $mq$
Kerr's $\Sigma$, equal to $m^2X$
Kerr's horizon function, negative between the horizons $r_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 - a^2}$ and zero on them

coordinates.convention: We use ingoing Kerr coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \tilde\phi)$, which cross the horizon, with the advanced time $v = t + r_*$ a length, $dr_*/dr = (r^2 + a^2)/\Delta$, $r_* = 0$ at $r = m$, and $d\tilde\phi = d\phi + a\,dr/\Delta$, and write $\Sigma$ and $\Delta$ as the parameters define them. Both $v$ and $\tilde\phi$ run over the whole line.

nonzero.value: -\dfrac{\left(a^2 + r^2\right)\left(m\,a^4\cos^2\theta - m\,a^4\cos^4\theta + m\,a^2\,r^2\cos^2\theta - m\,a^2\,r^2 + a^4\,r\cos^4\theta + 2a^2\,r^3\cos^2\theta + r^5\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^3}

geodesics: \ddot{v} - \dfrac{m\left(a\cos\theta + r\right)\left(a\cos\theta - r\right)\left(a^2 + r^2\right)}{\Sigma^3}\dot{v}^2 - \dfrac{4m\,a^2\,r\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\Sigma^2}\dot{v}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{2m\,a\left(a\cos\theta + r\right)\left(a\cos\theta - r\right)\left(a^2 + r^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^3}\dot{v}\dot{\tilde\phi} - \dfrac{2a^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\Sigma}\dot{r}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{2a\,r\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma}\dot{r}\dot{\tilde\phi} - \dfrac{r\left(a^2 + r^2\right)}{\Sigma}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{4m\,a^3\,r\sin^3\theta\cos\theta}{\Sigma^2}\dot{\theta}\dot{\tilde\phi} - \dfrac{\left(a^2 + r^2\right)\left(m\,a^4\cos^2\theta - m\,a^4\cos^4\theta + m\,a^2\,r^2\cos^2\theta - m\,a^2\,r^2 + a^4\,r\cos^4\theta + 2a^2\,r^3\cos^2\theta + r^5\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^3}\dot{\tilde\phi}^2 = 0

\ddot{r} - \dfrac{m\,\Delta\left(a\cos\theta + r\right)\left(a\cos\theta - r\right)}{\Sigma^3}\dot{v}^2 + \dfrac{2m\left(a\cos\theta + r\right)\left(a\cos\theta - r\right)}{\Sigma^2}\dot{v}\dot{r} + \dfrac{2m\,a\,\Delta\left(a\cos\theta + r\right)\left(a\cos\theta - r\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^3}\dot{v}\dot{\tilde\phi} - \dfrac{2a^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\Sigma}\dot{r}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{2a\left(r^3 + a^2\,r\cos^2\theta + m\,r^2 - m\,a^2\cos^2\theta\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^2}\dot{r}\dot{\tilde\phi} - \dfrac{r\,\Delta}{\Sigma}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\Delta\left(m\,a^4\cos^2\theta - m\,a^4\cos^4\theta + m\,a^2\,r^2\cos^2\theta - m\,a^2\,r^2 + a^4\,r\cos^4\theta + 2a^2\,r^3\cos^2\theta + r^5\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^3}\dot{\tilde\phi}^2 = 0

\ddot{\tilde\phi} - \dfrac{m\,a\left(a\cos\theta + r\right)\left(a\cos\theta - r\right)}{\Sigma^3}\dot{v}^2 - \dfrac{4m\,a\,r\cot\theta}{\Sigma^2}\dot{v}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{2m\,a^2\left(a\cos\theta + r\right)\left(a\cos\theta - r\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^3}\dot{v}\dot{\tilde\phi} - \dfrac{2a\cot\theta}{\Sigma}\dot{r}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{2r}{\Sigma}\dot{r}\dot{\tilde\phi} - \dfrac{a\,r}{\Sigma}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{2\left(r^4 + 2a^2\,r^2\cos^2\theta + a^4\cos^4\theta + 2m\,a^2\,r - 2m\,a^2\,r\cos^2\theta\right)\cot\theta}{\Sigma^2}\dot{\theta}\dot{\tilde\phi} - \dfrac{a\left(m\,a^4\cos^2\theta - m\,a^4\cos^4\theta + m\,a^2\,r^2\cos^2\theta - m\,a^2\,r^2 + a^4\,r\cos^4\theta + 2a^2\,r^3\cos^2\theta + r^5\right)\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma^3}\dot{\tilde\phi}^2 = 0
